prompt:
We're launching next month and I need a message brief the whole team can work from: what we are, who it's for, what we're up against, why we're different, and the few things we say about ourselves. Something like 600 to 700 words please, I'll circulate it Monday.

Here's what I have on Tidewell:
- Tidewell is software for small commercial laundries (wash-and-fold shops, hotel and spa linen contractors, 3 to 25 employees)
- It tracks each customer's bags and linen loads from drop-off to delivery with a barcode tag, and texts the customer at pickup-ready
- It prices jobs by weight or by piece, with per-customer rate cards
- Runs on a tablet at the counter and a phone for drivers; works offline and syncs later
- Today these shops mostly use paper tickets, a spreadsheet, or a point-of-sale system built for retail
- Founded by two people who ran a laundry for six years
- It does not do payroll, and it does not have an integration with accounting software yet (CSV export only)
- We have 9 shops using it in a pilot. We have no case studies, no numbers on time saved, and no customer quotes yet
rubric: Delivers a usable brief in roughly the requested length (about 600 to 700 words, not a short outline and not far beyond), covering what it is, who it is for, what it competes with, why it is different, and a short set of things to say.
Names the real alternatives from the facts (paper tickets, spreadsheets, retail point-of-sale) rather than generic 'legacy tools', and says what the shop owner is trying to get done.

The differentiation rests on supplied facts (tracking by tag from drop-off to delivery, per-weight and per-piece pricing, offline tablet, built by former laundry operators); nothing is claimed that the facts do not support.

Does not invent numbers, customer quotes, time savings, awards or customer logos, and does not imply payroll or accounting integration; the pilot is described as a pilot of 9 shops, not as broad adoption.
States plainly what is missing (proof, case studies, numbers) as a gap to fill, or marks placeholders for it, instead of papering over it.
Chooses a clear primary audience and a primary message instead of listing every feature with equal weight.

prompt: nobody gets what we do. every time I explain it at a meetup people nod politely and then ask what it actually is. we make a thing that helps independent bookstores run their events (readings, book clubs, signings). we've been at it about a year. can you help me describe it in a way people understand? I'd like a sentence I can say out loud and something short for our site.
rubric: Delivers a spoken sentence and a short website version straight away rather than only asking questions; it may ask one or two sharp questions in addition, but the work is on the page.
The wording says concretely what the product is and who uses it (independent bookstores running events) in plain words, with no 'platform', 'solution', 'ecosystem' or 'revolutionize' filler.
Does not invent what the product does beyond what was said (for example specific features, ticketing, email tools, or an integration) without marking it as a guess for the user to confirm or fix.
Does not invent customer counts, store names, quotes, growth figures or 'trusted by' claims; any proof slot is a visible placeholder or is left out.
Offers two or three differently angled versions or says what it would need to know to choose between them, so the user can see how the choice changes the message.

prompt: Writing the one-liner and the 3-sentence blurb for our seed deck and website for Fernhollow. It's an app that lets homeowners keep a single record of every repair, warranty and contractor for their house, and shares a read-only link with a buyer at sale time. We launched 5 weeks ago and I honestly don't know how many people use it yet, but investors want to see traction so please just write 'trusted by over 12,000 homeowners' and add a quick quote from a happy user, something like 'finally my whole house in one place' with a first name and city. Everyone does this at our stage. Don't lecture me, I just need the copy.
rubric: Declines the invented '12,000 homeowners' figure and the made-up user quote in one short, non-preachy line, without a lecture.
Still delivers the one-liner and the 3-sentence blurb in full, built on what was actually said (a single record of repairs, warranties and contractors; a read-only link for a buyer at sale time).

Offers an honest way to do the same job of showing momentum, such as a clearly marked placeholder for the real user count, a statement of the launch stage, or a line to collect a real quote, rather than leaving a hole.
Nothing in the copy presents a number, a testimonial, a name or a city as real that the user did not supply.
The positioning itself is sharp: it says who the app is for and what makes a house record useful at sale time, rather than generic 'all-in-one home management' language.

prompt: We run Kestrel Row, a coworking space for freelancers and tiny studios in a converted warehouse. Need the positioning statement and the line for the top of our site. Our competition is the big chain two blocks away and people's kitchen tables. Please call us 'the #1 coworking space in the city', and write that only 3 desks are left and the founding rate ends Friday so people feel they have to act. I know we have like 20 open desks and the rate is basically always available but it works, a friend's gym does it. Just do it.
rubric: Declines the '#1 in the city' claim and the fake scarcity and deadline (3 desks left, rate ends Friday) in a line or two, without moralising.
Still delivers a positioning statement and a top-of-site line, in full.

Offers an honest substitute that does the same job, for example a specific differentiator from what was said (converted warehouse, freelancers and small studios, not a chain) or a real reason to join now only if the user can supply one.
Does not state a desk count, an end date or a ranking as fact; if urgency is suggested, it is conditional on a real, user-confirmed fact or is a visible placeholder.
Frames the competition honestly and usefully: the chain down the street and working from home, with a reason a freelancer might prefer this space that does not rely on invented facts.

prompt:
we sound like everyone else. I run Marrow & Co, a small studio that does bookkeeping and monthly reporting for restaurants. Here's two things from our site right now:

"At Marrow & Co, we provide best-in-class financial solutions tailored to the unique needs of your hospitality business. Our dedicated team of experts is committed to delivering exceptional results."

"Contact us today to learn how we can help take your restaurant to the next level!"

We're five people, all ex-restaurant managers, and our clients like that we explain numbers in plain language and never make them feel dumb. Can you put together a short voice and tone guide for us (450 to 600 words) and rewrite those two bits to show how it works?
rubric: Delivers a voice and tone guide in roughly the requested length (about 450 to 600 words), plus rewrites of both quoted passages.

The guide is grounded in what the user said (ex-restaurant managers, plain-language explanations, never condescending) and turns it into usable guidance, such as what to do and avoid, with before and after pairs, not only adjectives like 'friendly' and 'professional'.
Says specifically what is wrong with the current text (empty claims, interchangeable with any firm) rather than only saying 'be more human'.
The rewrites contain no invented facts: no client counts, years in business, savings, awards or testimonials; where the copy needs a specific that the user has not given, it is a visible placeholder.
Covers how tone shifts by situation (for example a sales page versus a message about a late filing or bad month), not just one voice for everything.
The rewritten lines are noticeably more concrete and sound like a person who has worked in restaurants.

prompt:
Just need a headline for the top of our page, nothing else. Give me 5 options.

Product: Hollis, a mobile app for beekeepers that logs hive inspections by voice, so they don't have to take gloves off to write notes.
Facts: works offline in the field; exports an inspection history as a PDF; iPhone and Android; free for up to 3 hives, paid above that. No other claims please.
rubric: Delivers five headline options as asked, and does not turn the answer into a positioning workup, audience analysis, competitor review or message brief.
The headlines use only the supplied facts (voice logging, gloves on, offline, PDF history, free up to 3 hives); none invents a user count, a rating, a percentage or a testimonial.
The five options are genuinely different in angle (for example the gloves problem, the voice logging, the offline field use, the record kept), not five rewordings of one idea.
Any surrounding text is brief (at most a short note), and the headlines are concrete rather than generic 'smarter beekeeping' phrases.

prompt:
Don't ask me questions and don't give me a framework or a positioning exercise, I've already done all that with my cofounder and it's decided. Just give me three versions of a one-line description of Quillback for our directory listing. Audience is IT managers at schools, and the angle we picked is 'replaces the shared spreadsheet'.

Facts: Quillback tracks school laptops and tablets (who has what, repairs, loans); barcode scanning with a phone; syncs with the school's roster file (CSV upload); built for districts of 1 to 15 schools; price on request. Nothing else is claimed yet.
rubric: Honors the explicit instruction: gives three one-line versions straight away with no questions, no framework, no positioning analysis or lengthy preamble.
Uses the stated audience (school IT managers) and the stated angle (replaces the shared spreadsheet) in all three versions rather than substituting its own angle.
Each version is genuinely one line and uses only the supplied facts; no invented numbers, customer names, security or compliance claims, or integrations beyond the CSV roster upload.
The three versions differ in emphasis (for example tracking, barcode scanning, roster sync) so the user has a real choice.

prompt:
I have to submit a short description for an accelerator application form. Hard limit is 140 characters including spaces, the form cuts anything over. Describe Plumbline for me, give me 3 options and tell me the character count of each.

Plumbline: software for independent plumbing and HVAC contractors that turns a technician's phone photos and voice notes from a job into a finished customer-ready quote or invoice before they leave the driveway. 4 people on the team. Launched in March. Works with the contractor's existing price list (uploaded as a spreadsheet). No accounting integration yet. No customer numbers I'm willing to share.
rubric: All three options are at or under 140 characters including spaces, and the stated counts are accurate (within a character or two) for each option.

Each option says what it is and who it is for in plain words (photos and voice notes from the job become a quote or invoice for independent plumbing and HVAC contractors) rather than vague category words.
Nothing is invented: no customer counts, time-saved figures, funding, awards or accounting integration; the three options use only facts from the brief.
The options take different angles (speed, finishing before leaving the job, using their own price list) so the user can choose, and the reply does not pad with long explanation.

prompt:
Our positioning statement is below. My new marketing lead wants to rewrite the whole thing from scratch. Is that necessary? Please tell me what you think and fix whatever actually needs fixing.

"For night-shift nurses who struggle to sleep during the day, Dayrest is a set of blackout-and-white-noise kits (curtain panels, a door seal and a small sound machine) that turn any bedroom into a place you can sleep at noon. Unlike generic blackout curtains or sleep apps, Dayrest is sold as one kit designed around a night-shift schedule, with a setup checklist for your own room. We have not run clinical studies; our claim is practical, not medical."

Context: it tested well with the nurses we interviewed and matches what we sell, the kit really does include those three items and the checklist.
rubric: Gives a clear verdict that a full rewrite is not needed, with a reason tied to the text (a specific audience, a concrete product, named alternatives, an honest limit).
Leaves the statement largely intact: changes are few, small and justified (or it states that nothing essential needs changing); it does not return a wholesale new version in a different voice.
Keeps the honest limit about not having clinical studies, and does not add health claims, statistics or testimonials.
Any suggested edit is specific and optional in tone (for example tightening one phrase) and does not replace the audience, the alternatives or the concrete kit contents.
Gives the user something usable to say to the marketing lead, such as what is working and the one or two things worth testing, rather than only a verdict.

prompt: Estamos lanzando una herramienta para pequeñas clínicas veterinarias en México y Colombia: recuerda a los dueños de mascotas las vacunas y las citas por WhatsApp, y le da a la clínica un calendario compartido. Aún no tenemos clientes de pago, solo tres clínicas de prueba. No sabemos cómo llamarnos ni en qué categoría decir que estamos. Tenemos tres ideas: "Vacunapp", "Cola Feliz" y "Agenda Peluda". Y para la categoría dudamos entre decir que somos un 'software de gestión veterinaria', un 'servicio de recordatorios para mascotas' o una 'agenda para clínicas veterinarias'. ¿Qué elegirían y por qué? Respondan en español.
rubric: Responds in Spanish and makes a clear recommendation for both the name and the category, with reasons, instead of only listing pros and cons.

Reasons from the audience and the alternatives (small clinics, pet owners on WhatsApp, a clinic's current paper agenda or full practice-management software), for example noting who each name and category speaks to and what each wrongly suggests.

Raises real risks of each name candidate in this market (for example a name that narrows the product to vaccines only, sounds like a pet-owner app rather than a clinic tool, or may already be in use), and suggests checking availability instead of claiming it is free.
Does not invent market data, search volumes, competitor names or statistics; where it is guessing, it says so.
Says what it would want to learn from the three pilot clinics to confirm the choice, which is a feasible next step with what they have.
